input.idea:
How an AI agent really “thinks”. People imagine the AI does everything by itself. In my app TikMaker it works differently: the AI only chooses from a list, and plain code checks every answer it gives.

Example, step by step. First the AI picks one of 20 video templates and gives it a score from 1 to 5; the code checks the template really exists. Then it writes three hooks, and at least two must follow a proven formula from my list; if not, the code rejects the answer and asks again, up to three times. Then it writes the script, and the code checks it without any AI: every required scene is there, the video is not more than 15% too long, not too many words on screen. Finally it picks a layout for each scene from 61 frames taken from successful videos, and the AI never writes a single coordinate.

The lesson: the AI chooses, the code checks.

prompt.system:
You are the producer of a short-video channel (TikTok, Reels, Shorts).
Your job in this step: choose how the video will be told, by picking ONE template
from the list you are given. You do not write the video yet.

You get the channel, the video idea and the templates.
Pick the template whose "when to use" fits the idea best; the length matters less.
A template's "needs" are the facts its required scenes are built on. Pick one the idea
can fill with its OWN facts: a rise-to-success story needs a success to show, a how-to
needs steps, a list needs items. If the idea lacks what a template needs, that template
does not fit, however close its topic is.
Never invent a template: answer only with an id from the list.
score: 5 = made for this idea and the idea has every fact it needs, 3 = workable,
1 = nothing in the list fits.
reason: one or two sentences for the creator, in plain English, about this idea.
prompt.user:
Channel: TikMaker and AI coding. Mostly TikMaker itself: what it can do, how a video gets made with it, new features and how it is being built with AI (build in public). Around that, short concrete videos about other AI tools, vibe coding and Claude Code: one problem or one feature per video, shown on screen rather than told.
Audience: Creators who want to make short videos faster with AI, and developers or beginners who build apps with AI and want to work faster without breaking things.

Templates:
- id: analogy-explainer
  name: Explained with characters
  what: A concept explained through a small invented world or everyday analogy
  when to use: An idea that is an abstract concept (economics, health, finance) that becomes clear as a story.
  needs: problem, step, concept-term, real-case, lesson
  length: 26–63 s
- id: app-list
  name: Free apps list
  what: A quick list of apps, one per scene, each shown on screen
  when to use: An idea that recommends several apps or tools for one device or audience.
  needs: app-count, device-or-audience, app-name, app-feature
  length: 14–62 s
- id: brand-origin
  name: Rise of a brand
  what: From a humble start, through hardship, to a big brand
  when to use: An idea that is the history of a brand, product or founder that has already grown big: the idea gives the success to show (users, money, years). Not a creator telling why they built their own tool.
  needs: year-or-result, brand, founder, start, hardship, time-jump, result-number
  length: 43–80 s
- id: build-it-fast
  name: Build it fast
  what: Show the finished thing, then every step that built it
  when to use: An idea where the viewer can build something real in minutes with a tool.
  needs: result, time, tool-name, step, screen-recording
  length: 20–51 s
- id: dark-true-story
  name: Creepy true story
  what: A dark or strange true story told step by step to a shocking ending
  when to use: An idea that is a real crime, legend or eerie event.
  needs: place-or-person, event, ending
  length: 15–51 s
- id: explained-in-time
  name: Explained in 60 seconds
  what: A complex topic explained in a promised short time, often to an unlikely audience
  when to use: An idea that is a complex topic the viewer finds hard and wants explained quickly.
  needs: nothing special
  length: 35–54 s
- id: how-to-steps
  name: How-to steps
  what: A how-to promise followed by numbered steps on screen
  when to use: An idea that is a concrete task the viewer wants to do with a tool, in a few steps.
  needs: task, tool-name
  length: 32–43 s
- id: myth-vs-reality
  name: Myth vs reality
  what: What people think, then how it really works, with the proof
  when to use: An idea that corrects a common belief or reveals a hidden side of something familiar.
  needs: belief, background, reality, step, twist
  length: 26–59 s
- id: new-tool-news
  name: New tool news
  what: A just-released free tool, its benefits, a quick demo and a comment-keyword offer
  when to use: An idea that is news about a newly released or newly free tool.
  needs: who-released, tool-name, benefit, keyword, resource
  length: 30–107 s
- id: pain-to-fix
  name: Problem then fix
  what: The broken or painful way first, then the tool that fixes it, shown working
  when to use: An idea where a tool fixes a pain the audience recognises, including a creator telling why they built their own tool: the pain they had, then the tool that fixes it.
  needs: pain, task, screen-recording
  length: 30–40 s
- id: plot-recap
  name: Story recap
  what: A plot, journey or character backstory retold event by event
  when to use: An idea that recaps an episode, myth, game lore or a character's story.
  needs: story-name, setting, ending
  length: 48–181 s
- id: product-promo
  name: Product promo
  what: A product's benefits shown one by one through its interface, ending on where to get it
  when to use: An idea that promotes one product or service.
  needs: product-name
  length: 11–30 s
- id: question-answered
  name: Big question answered
  what: A why or how question, answered step by step with diagrams
  when to use: An idea that is a question the audience has wondered about.
  needs: question
  length: 43–71 s
- id: ranked-countdown
  name: Top N countdown
  what: Ranked items counted down to number one
  when to use: An idea that ranks a set of things by some measure.
  needs: rank-count, ranked-thing, rank-number, item-name, item-detail
  length: 25–60 s
- id: rapid-facts
  name: Rapid-fire facts
  what: Many short facts in a row, one per scene, with the strongest kept for last
  when to use: An idea that is a collection of short surprising facts around one theme.
  needs: theme, fact
  length: 40–56 s
- id: single-fact
  name: One surprising fact
  what: One fact built up line by line to a short reveal
  when to use: An idea that is a single surprising or eerie fact that fits in under 20 seconds.
  needs: topic
  length: 7–16 s
- id: software-tutorial
  name: Software how-to
  what: A finished result first, then the steps to make it in the software
  when to use: An idea that is a specific thing to make in a common program (PowerPoint, GitHub, a no-code tool).
  needs: result, software
  length: 14–53 s
- id: tool-deep-dive
  name: Tool explained
  what: What a tool is, how it differs, and what it really does
  when to use: An idea that explains one popular tool or model and how to think about it.
  needs: tool-name, difference, main-point
  length: 49–78 s
- id: tool-spotlight
  name: Tool spotlight
  what: One website or tool shown working, often as a numbered series part
  when to use: An idea that is a single useful website, repo or tool the viewer probably has not seen.
  needs: tool-category, series-part, screen-recording
  length: 10–56 s
- id: tool-tips-keyword
  name: Tool tips list
  what: Numbered tips for one tool, each named and then shown working, ending with a comment-keyword offer
  when to use: An idea that is a handful of concrete tips, skills or add-ons for one tool the audience already uses.
  needs: tool-name, tip-count, tip-number, tip-name, keyword, resource
  length: 47–88 s

prompt.system:
You write the opening line (hook) of a short vertical video (TikTok, Reels, Shorts):
the words shown and spoken in the first two seconds, which decide whether people keep watching.

Write THREE different hooks for the idea.
At least two must follow a formula from the list: fill the formula in for this idea,
do not copy its example. formulaId = that formula's id, or null for a hook of your own.
Fill a formula only with what the idea says: never claim something it does not
(no "I switched from…", no number, no result the idea does not give).
Each hook: one line, at most 12 words, plain spoken English, no hashtags, no emojis.
score: 5 = people stop scrolling, 3 = fine, 1 = weak.

Formulas:
- id: facts-you-didnt-know
  type: curiosity-gap
  formula: [Adjective] Facts YOU Didn't Know About [emoji] Part [N]
  example: Scary Facts YOU Didn't Know About 😨 Part 1
- id: dont-do-random-facts
  type: curiosity-gap
  formula: Don't [everyday action]. Random facts. The last fact is [adjective].
  example: Don't sleep with a chair near your bed.
- id: today-i-found-out
  type: curiosity-gap
  formula: Today I found out that a free [product] that almost everyone uses makes [result].
  example: Today I found out that a free extension that almost everyone uses makes $90 million in revenue.
- id: everyone-uses-but
  type: contrarian
  formula: Everyone's using [trending tool] to [goal], but [pain].
  example: Everyone's using Claude Code to build AI agents
- id: more-perfect-than-leader
  type: curiosity-gap
  formula: A more perfect [product type] than [market leader]
  example: A more perfect music player than spotify
- id: everyone-without-is-wasting
  type: contrarian
  formula: Everyone using [tool] without [feature] is just wasting their [resource].
  example: Everyone using Claude without skills is just wasting their tokens.
- id: if-youve-watched
  type: curiosity-gap
  formula: If you've watched [movie], then you've probably seen [detail].
  example: If you've watched Cars 2 then you've probably seen this scene of the Car Pope.
- id: you-are-the-only
  type: contrarian
  formula: You are the only [statement that sounds impossible].
  example: You are the only person alive.
- id: you-might-think
  type: contrarian
  formula: When you [everyday action], you might think [misconception]...
  example: When you visit a website, you might think that your computer is connecting with
- id: you-wont-believe
  type: curiosity-gap
  formula: You won't believe what [subject] did to [target]. Let me explain.
  example: You won't believe what this guy did to people. Let me explain.
- id: this-is-a-map-of
  type: curiosity-gap
  formula: This right here is a map of [unexpected thing].
  example: This right here is a map of the internet.
- id: extreme-but-scared
  type: curiosity-gap
  formula: This [character] literally [extreme action] but is too scared to [relatable action] because...
  example: This character literally trains with bears but is too scared to marry his crush because
- id: this-map-traces
  type: curiosity-gap
  formula: This map here traces [subject]'s [journey].
  example: This map here traces King Odysseus's ten year journey home, as told in Homer's epic poem, The Odyssey.
- id: brands-wouldnt-exist
  type: curiosity-gap
  formula: [Big brands] wouldn't exist today if [unlikely person] hadn't started [this brand].
  example: Campa Jeera, Lahori Jeera, ye sabhi bade brands aaj market mein dikhai bhi nahi dete agar Bengaluru ke is auto driver ne apne is brand ki shuruat na ki hoti.
- id: how-lowly-built-massive
  type: curiosity-gap
  formula: How a [humble person] built a [huge result].
  example: Aakhir kaise hotel mein jhoothe bartan dhone wale ladke ne khadi kar di 30 crore ki company
